title: Introduction to Node.js
subtitle: Server-side JavaScript — the event loop, V8, and your first Node program
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: JavaScript was originally browser-only. Building servers, CLIs, scripts, or accessing the file system required a different language (Python, Ruby, Java).
whyItExists.solution: Node.js embeds V8 (Chrome's JavaScript engine) with libuv (an async I/O library) to run JavaScript outside the browser. You use the same language for front-end and back-end, and Node's non-blocking I/O model makes it exceptionally good at handling many concurrent connections.
whyItExists.whenToUse: REST APIs, real-time apps (WebSockets, chat), build tools (Webpack, Vite, ESLint), CLIs, scripting, BFF (backend-for-frontend), microservices.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: CPU-intensive tasks like video encoding or complex mathematical computations — Node's single-threaded event loop can't parallelize these. Use Python with multiprocessing, Go, or worker_threads for CPU-bound work.

explainModes.beginner: Node.js lets you run JavaScript on your computer or a server — not just in a browser. With it, you can read files, talk to databases, and build web servers, all in JavaScript. It's like having a JavaScript engine that works everywhere.
explainModes.simple: Node.js = V8 (executes JS) + libuv (handles OS I/O asynchronously) + built-in modules (fs, path, http). The event loop: single-threaded, non-blocking. I/O operations (file read, network) are offloaded to libuv and callbacks are queued when done. Global objects: process (process info), __dirname (current dir path), __filename (current file path), global (like window in browser).
explainModes.standard: The event loop phases: timers (setTimeout/setInterval callbacks) → pending I/O → idle → poll (wait for I/O, execute callbacks) → check (setImmediate) → close callbacks. process.nextTick() runs before the next event loop iteration — highest priority async. Node 20 LTS supports full ES modules (import/export) and the --watch flag for auto-restart. Built-in test runner: node:test (no Jest/Mocha needed for basic tests).
explainModes.technical: libuv: a C library that provides an event loop, thread pool (for fs, crypto, DNS), and async I/O. The thread pool has 4 threads by default (UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE). Long CPU tasks in JS block the event loop — they prevent ALL other callbacks from running. This is why Node is great for I/O-bound but bad for CPU-bound. Worker threads (worker_threads module) let you run CPU work in parallel. The Cluster module forks the process to use multiple CPU cores.
explainModes.deepDive: V8 JIT compilation: JavaScript is compiled to machine code on first run (baseline JIT), then hot functions are optimized by a second compiler (Turbofan). Deoptimization: if a function's type profile changes (e.g., you start passing a string to a function that used to receive numbers), V8 deoptimizes and recompiles. Type consistency matters for performance. Node's module system: require() is synchronous, so circular requires work (the partially-constructed export is returned). ESM (import) is always async — top-level await is supported.

questions.question: Why is Node.js good at handling many simultaneous network connections?
options: Node.js uses multiple threads — one per connection
Node.js uses a single-threaded non-blocking event loop; I/O waits are offloaded to libuv so the thread is free to handle other requests
Node.js runs faster than other languages, so it handles more connections per second
Node.js automatically scales to multiple CPU cores
questions.explanation: Node.js uses a single-threaded event loop. When an I/O operation (database query, file read, HTTP request) starts, Node offloads it to libuv and immediately moves on to handle the next request — it doesn't wait. When the I/O completes, its callback is queued and run. This means one Node process can handle thousands of simultaneous connections without spawning one thread per connection.

faq.q: Should I use CommonJS (require) or ES Modules (import)?
faq.a: New projects should use ES Modules (import/export) — they're the standard. Set `"type": "module"` in package.json. CommonJS (require/module.exports) is older but still dominates the npm ecosystem. Many tutorials use CommonJS. Both work in Node.js 20; you can convert with the .mjs extension or the type field. Node's built-in modules work with both: `import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'` or `const { readFile } = require('fs/promises')`.
